The words

I brought my darkest sin to mind,
And called it by the vilest name,
And thought to fill my soul with grief,
When I had charged it with the blame; —
I said, "Before my God I'll fall,"
But sorrow came not at my call.

I said, "Ah, soul! the wrath of God
Shall smite the sinner with dismay,
The record of thy sin is kept,
And swiftly nears the reckoning day;" —
Methought I heard God's thunders roll,
But sorrow came not to my soul.

"Ah, stony heart! can thought of sin
In all its vileness bring no tears?
And canst thou hear God's thunders speak,
And weep not though the reckoning nears?"
I had no weeping to control,
For sorrow came not to my soul.

I looked, my Saviour looked at me,
O look of love no heart can bear!
Like raging torrents came my tears,
And plunged my spirit in despair;
Vain, vain my weeping to control,
For sorrow now hath found my soul.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Ab and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s (E♭), on the word “I”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 3/2 means three minim beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

John Brownlie translated these words from the Greek service books for Hymns from the Greek Office Books (Paisley, 1904).

The book printed the words without tunes. They are in Long Metre, six lines (8.8.8.8.8.8), and this page sets them to SELENA; any other Long Metre, six lines tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Traditional Greek
  • Translated (1904): John Brownlie (1857–1925)
  • Music (1850): Isaac B. Woodbury (1819–1858)

Tune SELENA by Isaac B. Woodbury (1819–1858); words by Traditional Greek; translated by John Brownlie (1857–1925).

Questions about I Brought My Darkest Sin to Mind

What is the doh of I Brought My Darkest Sin to Mind?

In this version, in Ab major, doh is Ab. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does I Brought My Darkest Sin to Mind start on?

It starts on s (E♭ in Ab major), a pickup on the word “I” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to s.

Is I Brought My Darkest Sin to Mind in the public domain?

Yes. John Brownlie died in 1925, Isaac B. Woodbury died in 1858; the words were in print by 1904 and the music in 1850. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
